options.why_wrong: Natriuretic peptides inhibit renin, aldosterone and sympathetic tone.

options.text: A rise in renal perfusion pressure
options.why_wrong: High renal perfusion pressure suppresses renin; low pressure stimulates it.

stem: Which of the following INCREASES renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells?

explanation: Dynamic exercise (running, cycling) is a volume load: heart rate and cardiac output rise greatly, SVR falls and diastolic pressure barely changes. Static exercise (lifting, handgrip) is a pressure load: systolic and diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure rise markedly with only a modest rise in heart rate and output. That afterload rise is why handgrip increases MR, VSD and AR murmurs.

options.text: A fall in systemic vascular resistance with an unchanged diastolic pressure: a volume load
options.why_wrong: That is the dynamic-exercise pattern; in static exercise contracting muscle compresses its own vessels, so SVR stays the same or rises.

options.text: A four-fold rise in cardiac output driven by a large rise in stroke volume
options.why_wrong: Static exercise raises cardiac output only modestly, and stroke volume changes little.

options.text: A fall in systolic pressure from vasodilatation in the working muscle
options.why_wrong: Blood pressure rises during isometric exercise; a fall in systolic pressure during exercise is a high-risk sign.

options.text: A marked rise in both systolic and diastolic pressure with little change in stroke volume: a pressure load

stem: Compared with the responses to dynamic exercise shown, what does sustained isometric handgrip produce?

explanation: By Fick, VO2 = HR × SV × (a-vO2 difference). Training expands plasma volume and enlarges a compliant LV, raising maximal stroke volume, and adds capillaries and mitochondria, widening O2 extraction. Maximal heart rate is not trainable; it falls with age.

options.text: A higher maximal stroke volume, together with a wider maximal arteriovenous O2 difference

options.why_wrong: Maximal heart rate is set by age and does not rise with training.

options.text: Better lung diffusing capacity, because VO2max in healthy people is limited by the lungs
options.why_wrong: In healthy people VO2max is limited mainly by maximal cardiac output, not by the lungs.

options.text: A higher resting heart rate, which raises cardiac output at rest
options.why_wrong: Training lowers the resting and submaximal heart rate (more vagal tone, larger stroke volume).

stem: After 6 months of endurance training, a healthy 30-year-old's VO2max has increased. What accounts for most of this increase?

explanation: Cardiac output = 180 × 0.1 L = 18 L/min. The a-vO2 difference = 20 − 5 = 15 mL/dL = 150 mL/L. VO2 = 18 L/min × 150 mL/L = 2,700 mL/min. Compared with rest (about 250 mL/min) this comes from about four-fold more cardiac output and three-fold more extraction.

options.why_wrong: This treats the a-vO2 difference of 15 mL/dL as if it were 15 mL/L; 15 mL/dL is 150 mL/L.
This converts litres to decilitres with a factor of 100 instead of 10.
This uses the arterial O2 content (20 mL/dL) instead of the arteriovenous difference.

stem: At peak exercise a subject has a heart rate of 180/min, a stroke volume of 100 mL, an arterial O2 content of 20 mL/dL and a mixed venous O2 content of 5 mL/dL. Using the Fick relation shown, what is the oxygen uptake?

explanation: Heart-rate recovery is the fall in heart rate in the first minute after exercise, driven by vagal reactivation. A fall of 12 beats/min or less with an upright cool-down (18 or less if the patient lies down at once) is abnormal and independently predicts mortality. Here the fall is only 8/min.

options.text: Abnormal heart-rate recovery, reflecting slow vagal reactivation; an adverse prognostic marker
A normal response: heart rate is expected to stay near its peak for several minutes
options.why_wrong: Heart rate normally falls quickly after exercise; a fall of 12/min or less in the first minute (upright) is abnormal.
Chronotropic incompetence is failure to reach 85% of the age-predicted maximum; 160/min is above that for a 55-year-old.

options.text: Excess vagal tone, as seen in endurance athletes
options.why_wrong: High vagal tone speeds heart-rate recovery; a slow fall means delayed vagal reactivation.

stem: A 55-year-old completes a symptom-limited treadmill test with an upright cool-down. His peak heart rate is 160/min, and 1 minute after stopping it is 152/min. What is the best interpretation?

explanation: This is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. PVR stays at or above systemic pressure, so blood shunts right-to-left across the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. With a ductal shunt, pre-ductal (right hand) saturation is higher than post-ductal (foot) saturation. Treatment includes oxygen, optimal ventilation, support of systemic pressure and inhaled nitric oxide, with ECMO when refractory.

options.text: Pulmonary vascular resistance has failed to fall, so desaturated blood shunts right-to-left across the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta
Transposition of the great arteries with pulmonary hypertension
options.why_wrong: The heart is structurally normal; transposition with pulmonary hypertension or arch obstruction gives reverse differential cyanosis (foot pinker than hand).

options.text: A left-to-right ductal shunt as pulmonary resistance falls
options.why_wrong: A left-to-right shunt sends oxygenated blood into the lungs and does not cause cyanosis.

options.text: Premature closure of the foramen ovale in utero
options.why_wrong: Pre-ductal and post-ductal saturations differ because of a shunt at ductal level, not because of foramen ovale closure.

stem: A term baby born after meconium aspiration is cyanosed. Right-hand SpO2 is 95% and foot SpO2 is 80%; echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Using the neonatal transition shown, what is the mechanism?

explanation: Oxygenated umbilical venous blood bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and enters the IVC. In the right atrium the Eustachian valve and the crista dividens stream it across the foramen ovale to the LA, LV and ascending aorta, so the coronary arteries and brain receive the best-oxygenated blood. Desaturated SVC blood goes to the RV and mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus.

options.text: The tricuspid valve, which channels IVC blood into the right ventricle
options.why_wrong: The desaturated SVC stream is the one that passes mainly through the tricuspid valve into the RV.

options.text: The ductus arteriosus, which draws blood from the right atrium
options.why_wrong: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta; it plays no part in atrial streaming.

options.text: The septum primum flap pressed against the septum secundum
options.why_wrong: The flap closing against the septum secundum is what shuts the foramen ovale after birth, when LA pressure exceeds RA pressure.

options.text: The Eustachian valve and the edge of the atrial septum (crista dividens)

stem: In the fetal circulation shown, what directs the well-oxygenated blood arriving through the ductus venosus and IVC across the foramen ovale into the left atrium?

explanation: In duct-dependent systemic circulation (hypoplastic left heart, critical coarctation, interrupted arch, critical AS) the body is perfused from the pulmonary artery through the ductus. Functional ductal closure in the first days causes shock. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) reopens and maintains the duct; apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension are its recognised side effects.

options.text: IV indomethacin to close the ductus arteriosus
options.why_wrong: Closing the duct would remove systemic blood flow, which depends on the duct in HLHS; COX inhibitors are for a significant PDA in preterm infants.

options.text: A prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the ductus arteriosus, with readiness to ventilate because it can cause apnoea
High-flow oxygen to reopen the ductus arteriosus
options.why_wrong: A rise in PaO2 constricts the ductus; oxygen does not reopen it.

options.text: Inhaled nitric oxide to lower pulmonary vascular resistance
options.why_wrong: Inhaled NO treats persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; it does not reopen the duct on which systemic flow depends.

stem: A 2-day-old baby with hypoplastic left heart syndrome becomes pale, mottled and acidotic with weak pulses. What is the immediate treatment?

explanation: LVOT area = 0.785 × 2.0² = 3.14 cm². Stroke volume = 3.14 × 18 = 56.5 mL. AVA = 56.5 / 90 = 0.63 cm², in the severe range (≤ 1.0 cm²). The dimensionless index 18 / 90 = 0.20 (< 0.25) agrees. Because D is squared, a 10% error in the LVOT diameter gives about a 20% error in the AVA.

options.why_wrong: This uses 0.785 × D (1.57 cm²) as the LVOT area; the diameter must be squared.
This uses π × D² as the LVOT area; the area is π × (D/2)², that is 0.785 × D².
0.20 is the dimensionless index (VTI ratio 18 / 90), which has no units; it is not the valve area.

stem: In a patient with aortic stenosis, the LVOT diameter is 2.0 cm, the LVOT VTI is 18 cm and the aortic valve VTI is 90 cm. Using the continuity equation shown, what is the aortic valve area?

explanation: Simplified Bernoulli: ΔP = 4v² = 4 × 3.5² = 4 × 12.25 = 49 mmHg. The proximal (LVOT) velocity of 0.8 m/s is low enough to ignore; it should be included when it is about 1.5 m/s or more. A peak velocity of 3.0-3.9 m/s is in the moderate range.

options.why_wrong: This multiplies the velocity by 4 without squaring it.
This squares 4v (14²) instead of multiplying 4 by v².
This squares the velocity but leaves out the factor of 4.

stem: Continuous-wave Doppler in a patient with aortic stenosis shows a peak aortic jet velocity of 3.5 m/s; the LVOT velocity is 0.8 m/s. What is the peak instantaneous gradient by the simplified Bernoulli equation?

explanation: This is classical low-flow, low-gradient AS (LVEF < 50%, SVi < 35 mL/m²). Dobutamine raises flow: in true severe AS the mean gradient reaches ≥ 40 mmHg (Vmax ≥ 4 m/s) while the AVA stays ≤ 1.0 cm²; in pseudo-severe AS the AVA rises above 1.0 cm². If stroke volume rises by less than 20% (no flow reserve), the CT calcium score is used.

options.text: A CT aortic valve calcium score as the first test
options.why_wrong: CT calcium scoring is the first confirmatory test in paradoxical low-flow AS with preserved EF; in classical low-flow AS it is used when dobutamine shows no flow reserve.

options.text: Classify the stenosis as moderate because the mean gradient is below 40 mmHg
options.why_wrong: At low flow the gradient underestimates severity; the gradient rises with the square of flow.

options.text: Calculate the valve area at rest with the Gorlin formula at cardiac catheterisation
options.why_wrong: The Gorlin formula is least reliable at low flow and does not test whether the valve area changes as flow rises.

stem: A 72-year-old man has an LVEF of 30%, an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm², a mean gradient of 25 mmHg and a stroke volume index of 28 mL/m². Measurements have been checked. Using the gradient-flow relation shown, what is the next step to grade the stenosis?

explanation: A tighter mitral valve holds up the LA-LV gradient for longer, so the pressure half-time lengthens. MVA ≈ 220 / PHT = 220 / 275 = 0.8 cm², which is severe (≤ 1.5 cm²). The estimate is unreliable straight after balloon mitral commissurotomy, with significant AR, or when LA or LV compliance is abnormal.

options.why_wrong: This divides the PHT by 220 instead of dividing 220 by the PHT.
The empirical constant is 220, not 100; MVA ≈ 220 / PHT.

options.text: The pressure half-time cannot estimate the mitral valve area; it is used only to grade aortic regurgitation
options.why_wrong: PHT is used in both lesions: it lengthens with tighter mitral stenosis and shortens with more severe AR.

stem: In a patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis, the pressure half-time of the transmitral Doppler signal is 275 ms. What is the estimated mitral valve area?

explanation: Isovolumetric contraction begins when the mitral valve closes (producing S1) and ends when the aortic valve opens. With both valves shut, pressure climbs steeply while volume stays constant (Guyton & Hall).

options.text: Both the mitral and aortic valves are closed and ventricular volume is constant
The aortic valve is open while ventricular volume falls
options.why_wrong: An open aortic valve means ejection has already begun — a later phase, not isovolumetric contraction.

options.text: The mitral valve is open while ventricular pressure falls
options.why_wrong: An open mitral valve with falling pressure describes diastolic filling, not isovolumetric contraction.

options.text: Ventricular volume rises steeply while pressure is unchanged
options.why_wrong: Volume cannot rise when both valves are shut; 'isovolumetric' means the volume is fixed.

stem: During isovolumetric contraction of the left ventricle, which statement is correct?

explanation: S1 marks closure of the atrioventricular (mitral then tricuspid) valves as the ventricles begin to contract — the start of isovolumetric contraction (Braunwald's Heart Disease).

options.text: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.why_wrong: Semilunar-valve closure produces S2, not S1.

options.text: Opening of the aortic valve at the start of ejection
options.why_wrong: Valve opening is normally silent; S1 is produced by AV-valve closure.

options.text: Rapid passive filling of the ventricle in early diastole
options.why_wrong: A sound from early rapid filling is S3, not S1.

stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by which event?

explanation: The dicrotic notch is the small upward deflection produced when the aortic valve snaps shut and blood briefly rebounds against it; it coincides with S2 and the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation.

options.text: Closure of the aortic valve, marking the start of isovolumetric relaxation
Opening of the aortic valve at the onset of ejection
options.why_wrong: Aortic valve opening starts ejection; the notch is a brief pressure rebound after valve closure.

options.text: Mitral valve opening at the start of ventricular filling
options.why_wrong: Mitral opening is a left-atrial/ventricular event and does not create the aortic incisura.
Peak systolic pressure occurs during ejection, before the valve closes.

stem: The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure tracing corresponds to:

explanation: S4 is a late-diastolic sound from atrial contraction ('atrial kick') against a stiff ventricle (e.g. LVH, ischaemia, HFpEF). Because it needs atrial contraction, S4 disappears in atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
Rapid early diastolic filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle
options.why_wrong: That mechanism produces S3, not S4.

options.text: Turbulent flow across a stenotic aortic valve
options.why_wrong: Turbulence across a valve produces a murmur, not an S4 gallop.

options.text: Closure of the pulmonary valve during inspiration
options.why_wrong: Delayed pulmonary closure causes physiological splitting of S2, not an S4.

stem: A fourth heart sound (S4) is best explained by:

explanation: The 'a' wave requires organised atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation there is no coordinated atrial systole, so the 'a' wave is lost. (Complete heart block gives cannon a waves; AF gives none.)

options.why_wrong: In complete heart block the atria still contract, intermittently against a closed tricuspid valve, producing intermittent giant 'cannon' a waves rather than absent a waves.
First-degree block merely delays conduction; atrial contraction and the a wave persist.
Sinus tachycardia preserves organised atrial contraction, so the a wave is present.

stem: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is caused by right atrial contraction. In which rhythm is the 'a' wave absent?

explanation: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV, which is the horizontal width of the PV loop. The enclosed area is stroke work and the ESPVR slope (Ees) indexes contractility (Braunwald's Heart Disease).

options.text: The width of the loop (end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume)
The height of the loop (peak systolic minus diastolic pressure)
options.why_wrong: The vertical dimension reflects pressures generated, not the volume ejected.

options.text: The area enclosed by the loop
options.why_wrong: The enclosed area represents stroke work, not stroke volume.

options.text: The slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship
options.why_wrong: That slope (Ees) indexes contractility, not stroke volume.

stem: On the left ventricular pressure-volume loop, the stroke volume is represented by:

explanation: Ees, the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship, is the classic relatively load-independent measure of contractility. Ejection fraction, SV and CO all vary with loading conditions.

options.text: The slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (Ees)

options.why_wrong: Ejection fraction is sensitive to preload and especially afterload, so it is load-dependent.
Stroke volume changes with preload and afterload independent of contractility.
Cardiac output depends on heart rate and loading conditions, not contractility alone.

stem: Which parameter is the most load-independent index of myocardial contractility?

explanation: Afterload is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject. Raising it (at fixed preload and contractility) shifts the aortic-valve-closure point up and to the right: the ventricle cannot eject as far, so ESV rises and SV falls (the beat-to-beat effect, before compensatory Frank-Starling on the next beat).

options.text: Increase end-systolic volume and decrease stroke volume
Decrease end-systolic volume and increase stroke volume
options.why_wrong: Higher afterload opposes ejection, so the ventricle ejects less and retains more blood.

options.text: Leave stroke volume unchanged because contractility is fixed
options.why_wrong: Even at fixed contractility, raising afterload reduces ejection (the loop ends at a higher ESV).

options.text: Increase stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism
options.why_wrong: Frank-Starling responds to preload (fibre length), not to an isolated afterload rise.

stem: At constant preload and contractility, an acute rise in afterload will:

explanation: Wall stress sigma = (P x r) / (2h). A dilated ventricle (large r) has high wall stress and oxygen demand; concentric hypertrophy (increased h) normalises wall stress. This underlies the afterload burden in hypertension and aortic stenosis.

options.text: Ventricular pressure and chamber radius, and inversely proportional to wall thickness
Wall thickness, and inversely proportional to chamber radius
options.why_wrong: The relationship is reversed: thicker walls LOWER wall stress, and larger radius RAISES it.
Laplace relates stress to pressure, radius and thickness, not directly to heart rate.

options.text: Blood viscosity and vessel length (Poiseuille's law)
options.why_wrong: Those are determinants of resistance to flow, not of ventricular wall stress.

stem: According to the law of Laplace, left ventricular wall stress is directly proportional to:

explanation: Preload is the degree of myocyte stretch at end-diastole, best represented by end-diastolic volume (clinically approximated by LVEDP or PCWP). It sets the operating point on the Frank-Starling curve.

options.why_wrong: MAP reflects the downstream pressure load (an afterload correlate), not preload.
SVR is a determinant of afterload, not a measure of preload.
Ejection fraction reflects ventricular emptying, not the end-diastolic filling volume.

stem: Which best estimates left ventricular preload?

explanation: MAP ~ DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) because the heart spends roughly two-thirds of each resting cycle in diastole. At fast heart rates diastole shortens and MAP moves closer to the arithmetic mean.

options.text: Diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure
The simple average of systolic and diastolic pressure
options.why_wrong: Diastole occupies about two-thirds of the cardiac cycle at rest, so a plain average overestimates MAP.

options.text: Systolic pressure minus one-third of the pulse pressure
options.why_wrong: This formula is upside down; MAP lies closer to the diastolic value, not the systolic value.

options.text: Pulse pressure multiplied by heart rate
options.why_wrong: That product has no physiological meaning as MAP.

stem: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is most accurately approximated at a normal resting heart rate by:

explanation: CO = HR x SV. Stroke volume itself is governed by preload, afterload and contractility (Guyton & Hall).

options.text: Stroke volume and systemic vascular resistance
options.why_wrong: SV x SVR is not cardiac output; MAP ~ CO x SVR relates pressure to flow and resistance.
Ejection fraction is a ratio (SV/EDV); CO needs an absolute volume per beat (SV).

options.text: Mean arterial pressure and heart rate
options.why_wrong: Pressure times rate is the rate-pressure product (an oxygen-demand index), not cardiac output.

stem: Cardiac output is the product of:

explanation: Frank-Starling: within physiological limits, greater preload stretches sarcomeres toward their optimal overlap (~2.2 micrometres) and raises myofilament calcium sensitivity, so a greater end-diastolic volume produces a stronger contraction and larger stroke volume.

options.text: Increasing end-diastolic fibre length increases the force of the next contraction and stroke volume
Increasing heart rate increases contractility (the staircase phenomenon)
options.why_wrong: Rate-dependent potentiation (Bowditch/Treppe) is a separate mechanism from Frank-Starling.

options.text: Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility independently of fibre length
options.why_wrong: That is beta-adrenergic (homeometric) regulation, not the length-dependent Frank-Starling effect.

options.text: Rising afterload reduces stroke volume on the same beat
options.why_wrong: That is the afterload effect, not the preload-driven Frank-Starling relationship.

stem: The Frank-Starling mechanism describes how:

explanation: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2). The A-V difference is 5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L. CO = 250 / 50 = 5 L/min (a normal resting value).

options.why_wrong: This is off by a factor of ten — the arteriovenous difference must be converted from mL/dL to mL/L (5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L).
This ignores the unit conversion and inverts the scale; such an output is physiologically impossible.
Halving the true value suggests using 10 mL/dL rather than the correct 5 mL/dL A-V difference.

stem: Using the Fick principle, a patient has an oxygen consumption of 250 mL/min, arterial O2 content 20 mL/dL and mixed venous O2 content 15 mL/dL. The cardiac output is approximately:

explanation: Reduced contractility in HFrEF shifts the Frank-Starling curve down and to the right: the ventricle needs a much higher filling pressure to generate a modest stroke volume, which is why congestion develops.

options.text: Shifted downward and flattened, so a given preload generates a smaller stroke volume
Shifted upward and leftward, generating more stroke volume at any preload
options.why_wrong: An upward-left shift indicates increased contractility (e.g. catecholamines), the opposite of failure.

options.text: Unchanged, with heart failure due solely to valve disease
options.why_wrong: Reduced contractility in systolic HF depresses the curve regardless of valve status.

options.text: Steeper, so small preload changes cause large stroke-volume swings
options.why_wrong: The failing ventricle is less preload-responsive, giving a flatter not steeper curve.

stem: In systolic heart failure, the Frank-Starling curve is characteristically:

explanation: EF = SV/EDV = (EDV - ESV)/EDV, normally about 55-70%. It is a load-dependent measure of ventricular emptying, widely used to classify heart failure (HFrEF vs HFpEF) per ESC guidance.

options.text: Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume
Stroke volume divided by end-systolic volume
options.why_wrong: The denominator is end-diastolic (total filling) volume, not end-systolic volume.
That difference is the stroke volume itself, not the ejection fraction (a ratio).

options.text: Cardiac output divided by heart rate
options.why_wrong: CO/HR gives stroke volume, not ejection fraction.

stem: Left ventricular ejection fraction is defined as:

explanation: Phase 0 of fast-response cells (atrial, ventricular, His-Purkinje) is the steep depolarisation from the rapid inward Na+ current. Class I antiarrhythmics block this channel.

options.text: A fast inward sodium current through voltage-gated Na+ channels

options.why_wrong: The L-type Ca2+ current drives the slow upstroke of nodal cells and the plateau of fast cells, not the rapid phase-0 upstroke here.
Outward K+ currents repolarise the cell (phases 1 and 3); they do not depolarise it.
If drives spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation in pacemaker cells, not phase 0 of working myocardium.

stem: In a ventricular (fast-response) action potential, the rapid upstroke of phase 0 is produced by:

explanation: During phase 2, inward Ca2+ (L-type) current nearly balances outward K+ current, holding the membrane near 0 mV. This plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release and gives the long refractory period.

options.text: Inward L-type calcium current balanced by outward potassium current
A sustained inward sodium current with no potassium efflux
options.why_wrong: Phase-0 Na+ channels inactivate quickly; the plateau is a Ca2+/K+ balance, not sustained Na+.

options.text: Pure outward potassium current driving repolarisation
options.why_wrong: Unopposed K+ efflux produces phase 3 (repolarisation), not the plateau.

options.text: Electrogenic activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase only
options.why_wrong: The pump contributes to the resting potential but does not create the plateau.

stem: The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is maintained mainly by:

explanation: The SA node has an unstable diastolic potential because of the funny current (If) plus T-type Ca2+ influx and declining K+ efflux. If is the target of ivabradine, which slows heart rate without affecting contractility.

options.text: The funny current (If), an inward Na+ current activated on hyperpolarisation
A large inward fast Na+ current as in ventricular cells
options.why_wrong: SA nodal cells have few functional fast Na+ channels; their pacemaker drift is the If current.

options.text: Inward rectifier K+ (IK1) maintaining a stable resting potential
options.why_wrong: Strong IK1 would prevent spontaneous drift; nodal cells have little IK1, allowing pacemaking.
Chloride currents are not the principal pacemaker mechanism of the SA node.

stem: Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation of the sinoatrial node is driven predominantly by:

explanation: AV-nodal conduction is slow (upstroke driven by L-type Ca2+ current), producing the PR-interval delay that lets the atria finish filling the ventricles before ventricular systole. The His-Purkinje system is the fastest-conducting tissue.

options.why_wrong: The His-Purkinje network has the FASTEST conduction, rapidly activating the ventricles.
Atrial muscle conducts faster than the AV node; it is not the rate-limiting delay.
The SA node is the pacemaker; the deliberate conduction delay occurs at the AV node.

stem: Which component of the conduction system has the SLOWEST conduction velocity, creating the physiological delay between atrial and ventricular contraction?

explanation: The pacemaker hierarchy descends in rate: SA node 60-100, AV junction 40-60, ventricular/His-Purkinje 20-40 per minute. The fastest pacemaker (SA) sets the rhythm and overdrive-suppresses the slower ones.

options.why_wrong: The hierarchy is reversed: the most proximal tissue (SA node) has the fastest intrinsic rate.
These rates are all too high; they describe tachycardias, not intrinsic escape rates.
Each subsidiary pacemaker is progressively slower than the one above it, which is why the SA node normally dominates.

stem: The intrinsic (escape) pacemaker rates of the conduction system are approximately:

explanation: The long plateau keeps fast Na+ channels inactivated, so the cell cannot generate another upstroke until it repolarises and the channels recover. This effective refractory period prevents tetany and limits re-entry.

options.text: Its fast sodium channels are inactivated, producing the effective refractory period
Its resting membrane potential is maximally negative
options.why_wrong: During the plateau the membrane is near 0 mV, not maximally negative; refractoriness is due to Na+ channel inactivation.
Refractoriness is intrinsic to channel kinetics, not dependent on vagal input.

options.text: The Na+/K+-ATPase is temporarily switched off
options.why_wrong: The pump is not the basis of the refractory period; inactivated Na+ channels are.

stem: Why can a ventricular myocyte not be re-excited during the plateau of its action potential?

explanation: Contraction of the LV squeezes the vessels running through its wall (especially the subendocardium), so most LV coronary flow happens in diastole. Tachycardia shortens diastole and is a key cause of subendocardial ischaemia (the right ventricle, under lower pressure, is perfused in both phases).

options.text: Diastole, when the compressive force on intramural vessels is lowest
Systole, when aortic pressure is highest
options.why_wrong: Although aortic pressure peaks in systole, LV contraction compresses the intramural coronary vessels, so LV perfusion is throttled during systole.
LV coronary flow is strongly phasic because of systolic compression; it is not uniform.
That brief phase is when compression begins to impede flow, not when most perfusion occurs.

stem: Blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs predominantly during:

explanation: The subendocardium faces the highest wall stress and the greatest systolic compression, and it is perfused last, so it is the most vulnerable layer. Subendocardial ischaemia produces ST depression; transmural ischaemia produces ST elevation.

options.why_wrong: The subepicardium has the most favourable perfusion; the subendocardium is the first to suffer.
Ischaemic vulnerability is greatest at the subendocardium, not uniform across the wall.
Epicardial fat is not myocardium and is not the relevant ischaemic territory.

stem: Which region of the ventricular wall is most vulnerable to ischaemia?

explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure - LVEDP. A high LVEDP (failing or stiff ventricle) or a low aortic diastolic pressure (e.g. aortic regurgitation, hypotension) narrows this gradient and worsens subendocardial ischaemia.

options.text: Aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
Aortic systolic pressure minus right atrial pressure
options.why_wrong: LV subendocardial perfusion occurs in diastole, so diastolic (not systolic) aortic pressure is the driving head, and LVEDP (not RAP) is the back-pressure.

options.text: Mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure
options.why_wrong: This generic formula ignores the phasic, diastole-dependent nature of LV coronary perfusion.

options.text: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure minus LVEDP
options.why_wrong: Neither term represents the aortic driving pressure for coronary flow.

stem: Effective subendocardial coronary perfusion pressure for the left ventricle is best represented by:

explanation: Myocardial oxygen demand rises with heart rate, contractility and wall stress (afterload/preload). The rate-pressure product (HR x systolic BP) is a convenient clinical surrogate. Supply depends on coronary flow and arterial oxygen content.

options.text: Heart rate, contractility and ventricular wall stress
Coronary artery diameter, haemoglobin and arterial O2 saturation
options.why_wrong: Those govern oxygen SUPPLY, not demand.

options.text: Preload, blood viscosity and plasma oncotic pressure
options.why_wrong: These are not the recognised determinants of myocardial oxygen consumption.

options.text: Respiratory rate, tidal volume and PaO2
options.why_wrong: Ventilatory parameters set systemic oxygenation, not myocardial oxygen demand.

stem: Which combination lists the principal determinants of myocardial oxygen DEMAND?

explanation: The heart extracts most of the oxygen it is offered even at rest, so increased demand is met almost entirely by increasing flow. Local metabolites (adenosine, CO2, H+, low PO2) relax coronary resistance vessels; this metabolic autoregulation is the basis of coronary flow reserve.

options.text: Local metabolic vasodilation (e.g. adenosine, lowered PO2) of the coronary microvasculature
A large increase in myocardial oxygen extraction
options.why_wrong: Myocardial oxygen extraction is already near-maximal at rest, so extra demand must be met by more flow, not more extraction.
Vasoconstriction would reduce, not increase, coronary flow; metabolic vasodilation dominates.

options.text: A fall in aortic diastolic pressure increasing the perfusion gradient
options.why_wrong: A lower diastolic pressure would reduce the perfusion gradient, not augment flow.

stem: During exercise, the several-fold increase in coronary blood flow needed to match demand is achieved mainly by:

explanation: The resting rate (~70) is slower than the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100-110) because of constant vagal tone. Atropine blocks M2 receptors and removes this brake, so the rate climbs toward the intrinsic rate.

options.text: Blocks M2 muscarinic receptors, removing resting vagal (parasympathetic) tone
Directly stimulates beta-1 receptors on the SA node
options.why_wrong: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, not a beta-agonist; it unmasks the intrinsic rate rather than stimulating the node.
Atropine does not augment sympathetic transmitter release; it blocks the vagal brake.

options.text: Blocks the funny current to speed phase-4 depolarisation
options.why_wrong: Blocking If (as ivabradine does) would SLOW the heart, the opposite of atropine's effect.

stem: A healthy adult with a resting heart rate of 72/min is given intravenous atropine and the rate rises to about 105/min. This occurs because atropine:

explanation: Lusitropy is the rate of myocardial relaxation. Beta-1 -> Gs -> cAMP -> PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, relieving its inhibition of SERCA2a, so calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum faster and the ventricle relaxes sooner — important for filling when heart rate is high.

options.text: PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban, speeding SERCA-mediated calcium reuptake into the SR
Slower calcium reuptake prolonging the plateau
options.why_wrong: Slower reuptake would impair relaxation (negative lusitropy), the opposite of the beta-1 effect.

options.text: Opening of M2-gated potassium channels in the ventricle
options.why_wrong: That is a vagal (parasympathetic) action and has little effect on ventricular relaxation.

options.text: Increased myofilament calcium sensitivity from fibre stretch
options.why_wrong: That describes length-dependent activation (Frank-Starling), not catecholamine-driven lusitropy.

stem: Positive lusitropy produced by sympathetic (beta-1) stimulation of the heart results from:

explanation: Right vagus -> SA node (rate); left vagus -> AV node (conduction). Parasympathetic fibres richly supply the nodes and atria but only sparsely the ventricles, so the vagus has a large effect on rate/conduction and little direct effect on ventricular force.

options.text: The right vagus mainly supplies the SA node (rate) and the left vagus mainly the AV node (conduction)
The vagus densely innervates the ventricular myocardium and strongly reduces contractility
options.why_wrong: Vagal supply to the ventricles is sparse; the major vagal effects are on rate and AV conduction.

options.text: The left vagus chiefly controls heart rate at the SA node
options.why_wrong: It is the RIGHT vagus that predominantly controls SA-nodal rate.

options.text: Vagal fibres release noradrenaline onto beta-1 receptors
options.why_wrong: Vagal (parasympathetic) fibres release acetylcholine onto M2 receptors, not noradrenaline.

stem: Regarding vagal innervation of the heart, which statement is correct?

explanation: Digoxin's rate-slowing effect in AF is largely indirect and vagotonic: enhanced parasympathetic tone prolongs AV-nodal refractoriness. (Its positive inotropy is a separate action via Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition.) Because the effect is vagal, it is overridden by the high sympathetic drive of exertion.

options.text: Increasing vagal (parasympathetic) tone, which slows AV-nodal conduction
Blocking beta-1 adrenergic receptors at the AV node
options.why_wrong: Digoxin is not a beta-blocker; its rate-control action is a vagotonic (cholinergic) effect.

options.text: Directly blocking L-type calcium channels like verapamil
options.why_wrong: Calcium-channel blockade is the mechanism of non-dihydropyridines, not digoxin.

options.text: Inhibiting the funny current in the SA node
options.why_wrong: If inhibition is ivabradine's mechanism and does not explain AV-nodal rate control in AF.

stem: Digoxin slows the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation primarily by:

explanation: Beta-1 -> Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> PKA, which phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban and If channels to raise rate, contractility, conduction and relaxation. Beta-blockers interrupt this pathway.

options.text: Gs protein -> adenylyl cyclase -> increased cAMP -> protein kinase A

options.why_wrong: Gi lowers cAMP and is the pathway of M2 and alpha-2 receptors, which slow or inhibit, not beta-1.
The Gq/IP3 pathway is used by alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction), not cardiac beta-1 receptors.

options.text: Direct ligand-gated opening of a sodium channel
options.why_wrong: Adrenergic receptors are G-protein-coupled, not ligand-gated ion channels.

stem: Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors increases heart rate and contractility through which signalling pathway?

explanation: M2 -> Gi lowers cAMP (slowing the funny current and L-type Ca2+ current) and the Gi beta-gamma subunit opens GIRK/I_KACh potassium channels. The resulting K+ efflux hyperpolarises the node and flattens phase 4, producing negative chronotropy and dromotropy.

options.text: Couple to Gi, lowering cAMP and opening acetylcholine-gated K+ channels (hyperpolarisation)
Couple to Gs, raising cAMP and the funny current
options.why_wrong: Raising cAMP would speed the node; M2 couples to Gi and slows it.

options.text: Couple to Gq, raising intracellular calcium
options.why_wrong: Gq/IP3 signalling is used by alpha-1 receptors, not nodal M2 receptors.

options.text: Block fast sodium channels in the SA node
options.why_wrong: SA-nodal pacing does not depend on fast Na+ channels, and M2 acts through G-proteins, not channel block.

stem: Acetylcholine slows the sinoatrial node by acting on M2 receptors, which:

explanation: Alpha-1 -> Gq -> phospholipase C -> IP3/DAG -> raised intracellular Ca2+ -> vasoconstriction, which increases SVR and arterial pressure. The pressure rise often triggers a reflex (baroreflex) bradycardia.

options.text: Gq-mediated vascular smooth-muscle contraction, increasing systemic vascular resistance

options.why_wrong: Alpha-1 does not act through Gs on the heart; its pressor effect is vascular vasoconstriction via Gq.
Vasodilation would lower, not raise, blood pressure; alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction.

options.text: Blocking M2 receptors at the SA node
options.why_wrong: Muscarinic blockade affects heart rate, not the vasoconstrictor pressor response of alpha-1.

stem: Phenylephrine, a selective alpha-1 agonist, raises blood pressure mainly by:

explanation: Central alpha-2 agonism (clonidine, methyldopa) provides negative feedback that reduces sympathetic outflow from the brainstem, lowering heart rate and vascular tone. Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

options.text: Stimulating central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow
Blocking peripheral alpha-1 receptors to cause vasodilation
options.why_wrong: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist acting centrally, not an alpha-1 blocker like prazosin.

options.text: Antagonising beta-1 receptors in the heart
options.why_wrong: Clonidine is not a beta-blocker; it reduces central sympathetic drive via alpha-2 agonism.
Its action is neural (reduced sympathetic outflow), not direct arteriolar smooth-muscle relaxation.

stem: Clonidine lowers blood pressure principally by:

explanation: Higher arterial pressure stretches carotid-sinus and aortic-arch baroreceptors, increasing afferent firing to the NTS. The medulla then raises vagal tone and lowers sympathetic tone, reducing heart rate, contractility and SVR so pressure returns toward its set point.

options.text: Increasing vagal output and decreasing sympathetic output, lowering heart rate and SVR
Increasing sympathetic output to further raise blood pressure
options.why_wrong: That is positive feedback; the baroreflex is a negative-feedback buffer that opposes the pressure rise.

options.text: Decreasing baroreceptor firing as pressure rises
options.why_wrong: Higher pressure stretches the receptors MORE, so firing increases, not decreases.
A rise in pressure produces reflex bradycardia; tachycardia is the response to a FALL in pressure.

stem: A sudden rise in arterial blood pressure triggers the baroreflex, which responds by:

explanation: Carotid sinus -> glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, via the nerve of Hering); aortic arch -> vagus (CN X). Both converge on the nucleus tractus solitarius. This distinction is a classic exam discriminator.

options.why_wrong: The vagus carries afferents from the AORTIC ARCH baroreceptors; the carotid sinus uses CN IX.
CN V is sensory to the face and is not involved in the baroreflex afferent limb.
CN VII is not part of the baroreceptor pathway.

stem: Afferent signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla via which cranial nerve?

explanation: External pressure on the carotid sinus is read by the baroreflex as a pressure rise, so the medulla boosts vagal output to the AV node. The resulting AV slowing can break AV-nodal-dependent re-entry (AVNRT/AVRT) or unmask atrial activity.

options.text: Raises the pressure sensed at the carotid sinus, reflexly increasing vagal tone and slowing AV-nodal conduction
Mechanically compresses the SA node to reset it
options.why_wrong: The manoeuvre works through the baroreflex, not by physically compressing the pacemaker.

options.text: Reduces baroreceptor firing and withdraws vagal tone
options.why_wrong: Applying pressure INCREASES sensed pressure and vagal tone; it does not withdraw it.

options.text: Blocks sympathetic outflow to the ventricular myocardium directly
options.why_wrong: Its therapeutic effect is enhanced vagal slowing of the AV node, not direct sympathetic blockade.

stem: Carotid sinus massage can terminate some supraventricular tachycardias because it:

explanation: Inferior MI (usually RCA) stimulates vagally innervated inferoposterior LV C-fibre receptors, triggering the Bezold-Jarisch reflex: bradycardia, hypotension and vasodilation. RCA supply to the SA/AV nodes adds to the bradycardia. It often responds to atropine and fluids.

options.text: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (bradycardia, hypotension and vasodilation from inferior-LV receptor stimulation)

options.why_wrong: The Bainbridge reflex raises heart rate in response to atrial stretch; it does not cause bradycardia.
Cushing's reflex is driven by raised intracranial pressure and produces hypertension, not an MI-related hypotension.
The classic MI picture of brady-hypotension is the Bezold-Jarisch reflex (and RCA nodal ischaemia), not a primary chemoreceptor response.

stem: A patient with an acute inferior STEMI develops marked bradycardia and hypotension. Which reflex best explains this combination?

explanation: The Cushing reflex: dangerously high ICP produces brainstem ischaemia and a massive sympathetic surge (hypertension); the baroreflex answers the hypertension with bradycardia, and brainstem compression causes irregular respiration. It signals impending herniation.

options.text: Raised intracranial pressure causing a brainstem sympathetic surge with reflex bradycardia

options.why_wrong: Cardiogenic shock causes hypotension and tachycardia, not hypertension with bradycardia.

options.text: Septic shock with a hyperdynamic circulation
options.why_wrong: Sepsis typically produces low SVR, hypotension and tachycardia, the opposite of the Cushing triad.

options.text: A normal baroreflex response to hypovolaemia
options.why_wrong: Hypovolaemia lowers BP and raises HR; the Cushing triad is a sign of a neurological emergency.

stem: A head-injured patient shows rising blood pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing. This Cushing triad indicates:

explanation: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia arises from cyclical changes in vagal tone (inspiration transiently reduces vagal tone, raising heart rate). It is a normal finding, most pronounced in the young and fit, and its loss (reduced heart-rate variability) is an adverse prognostic sign.

options.text: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia — a normal variation reflecting healthy vagal tone

options.why_wrong: Sick sinus syndrome is a pathological sinus-node disorder, not the benign respiratory variation seen in healthy young people.
The phenomenon is rate modulation by vagal tone, not a conduction block at the AV node.
AF is irregularly irregular and chaotic; respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a smooth, breathing-linked variation.

stem: The beat-to-beat quickening of heart rate during inspiration and slowing during expiration in a healthy young adult is called:

explanation: The Bainbridge reflex: stretch of right-atrial receptors by increased venous return raises heart rate, helping the heart keep pace with incoming volume. It is most influential when the baseline heart rate is low, and can oppose the baroreflex.

options.text: The Bainbridge reflex (atrial stretch increasing heart rate)
The baroreflex responding to increased arterial pressure
options.why_wrong: The baroreflex would SLOW the heart if arterial pressure rose; the rate increase here is the atrial-stretch (Bainbridge) response.
Bezold-Jarisch causes bradycardia and hypotension, not a rate increase.
The Cushing reflex relates to raised intracranial pressure, not to volume loading of the atrium.

stem: A rapid intravenous fluid bolus raises right atrial filling and is followed by a small increase in heart rate. Which reflex accounts for this?

explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors sense hypoxaemia (low PaO2), hypercapnia and acidosis. Their main reflex effect is to drive ventilation; the direct cardiac effect of hypoxic stimulation is bradycardia with sympathetic vasoconstriction, usually masked by a secondary tachycardia from increased lung inflation.

options.text: A fall in arterial PaO2 (with contributions from a rise in PaCO2 and a fall in pH)

options.why_wrong: Chemoreceptors are activated by LOW oxygen, not high oxygen.

options.text: A rise in arterial blood pressure
options.why_wrong: Pressure changes stimulate baroreceptors, not chemoreceptors.
Temperature is not the primary stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors.

stem: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are stimulated primarily by:
